interactions.label: By mechanism of action, firearms are classified into which three groups?

params.question: By mechanism of action, firearms are classified into which three groups?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Handgun, shoulder arm, and country-made weapon is a classification by weapon CATEGORY, not by mechanism of action. Mechanism refers to how the weapon loads and fires successive rounds.

Correct. Single-shot weapons require manual reloading after each discharge; repeating/semi-automatic weapons self-load between shots; automatic weapons fire continuously while the trigger is held. This mechanistic grouping is the first step in identifying a firearm from wound characteristics.

Smooth-bore versus rifled is classification by BARREL CHARACTER, not mechanism of action. Smooth-bore barrels (shotguns) lack internal grooves; rifled barrels (pistols, rifles) have spiral grooves that spin the projectile for accuracy.

Revolver, pistol, and shotgun are specific weapon types, not mechanism-based categories. A revolver and a pistol are both handguns but differ in their loading mechanism (revolving cylinder versus magazine-fed slide).

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the classification scheme: mechanism of action divides firearms into single-shot (manual reload), repeating/semi-automatic (self-loading), and automatic (continuous fire). This is distinct from barrel character (smooth-bore vs rifled) or weapon category (handgun vs shoulder arm).

Well recalled. The three mechanistic groups — single-shot, repeating/semi-automatic, and automatic — determine how quickly successive rounds can be fired and thus how many wounds to expect in a rapid-fire incident.

params.question: A gunshot entrance wound shows dense sooty blackening over a 5 cm radius with singeing of surrounding hair, but NO tattooing (stippling) is visible. Which range of fire is MOST consistent with these findings?

answers.text: Contact range — all discharge products are deposited beneath the skin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: At contact range the muzzle is pressed against the skin and discharge products (soot, gases, unburnt powder) enter BENEATH the skin through the wound track. External sooty blackening on the surrounding skin surface, as described here, is inconsistent with a pure contact wound.

answers.text: Close range (within approximately 15 cm of the muzzle)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. At close range the discharge products (flame, soot, unburnt powder) travel as a compact mass and deposit ON the skin surface, producing visible blackening and singeing. Tattooing (stippling from discrete powder grains striking skin) has not yet appeared as a separate feature because the particles have not dispersed from the main gas column at this short distance.

Intermediate range is characterised by the PRESENCE of tattooing (stippling) and the ABSENCE of blackening — the exact opposite of the findings described. At intermediate range, soot has dissipated but individual powder grains still reach the skin.

answers.text: Distant range — only the bullet reaches the target

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: At distant range NO discharge products (soot, tattooing, singeing) are found on the skin — only the bullet strikes the body. This wound shows prominent blackening and singeing, ruling out distant range entirely.

overallFeedback.feedback: Think through the range categories systematically: contact (products beneath skin), close (soot and singeing on skin, no tattooing), intermediate (tattooing only, no soot), distant (no products at all). Match each finding in the question to the category whose features it fits.

Excellent analysis. The combination of sooty blackening and singeing WITHOUT tattooing places this wound in the close-range category — the products deposit on the skin surface as a compact mass before individual powder grains have dispersed.

params.question: A revolver recovered at a crime scene has its serial number completely obliterated. Which of the following is the MOST accurate medicolegal interpretation of this finding?

answers.text: The weapon cannot be linked to any registered owner and must be excluded from evidence

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An obliterated serial number does NOT render the weapon inadmissible as evidence. The firearm itself, its ballistic characteristics, and recovered cartridge cases remain valid forensic exhibits. Modern techniques such as acid etching may even recover the obliterated number.

answers.text: The serial number was likely worn away by routine use and carries no forensic significance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Stamped or engraved serial numbers do not obliterate through normal use. Complete obliteration indicates deliberate effort (filing, grinding, or chemical treatment) and is itself forensically and legally significant.

answers.text: Obliteration of the serial number is itself an offence under the Arms Act 1959, indicating illicit modification

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Under the Arms Act 1959, erasure or obliteration of a firearm's serial number is a criminal offence in its own right. This finding must be documented as it provides independent evidence of illicit modification — separate from the shooting incident — and may indicate unlawful possession or trafficking.

answers.text: The weapon was manufactured before serial number regulations and is therefore classified as an antique

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Indian firearms regulations have long mandated serial numbering. Complete obliteration implies deliberate removal, not absence of original marking. A genuinely antique weapon would show age-related wear patterns rather than signs of deliberate erasure.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: obliteration of a firearm's serial number is itself an offence under the Arms Act 1959. It indicates illicit modification and must be documented as an independent finding. The weapon remains admissible as evidence regardless of whether the serial number is legible.

Correct. Recognising that serial number obliteration is both a forensic finding and an independent criminal offence under the Arms Act 1959 is essential for complete medicolegal documentation of recovered firearms.
